item.title: OpenRouter reports data processing incidents on multiple inference providers, off-boards three and removes 125 endpoints from zero data retention eligibility [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenRouter disclosed that security researchers identified data processing incidents involving several inference providers, prompting OpenRouter to off-board three providers and remove 125 endpoints from its Zero Data Retention (ZDR) program. The company confirmed no breach or unauthorized access occurred on its own platform and has notified all potentially affected customers. OpenRouter is collaborating with researchers and providers to investigate the findings and is implementing ongoing testing and network path verification to prevent future incidents. The company requires validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any affected endpoints and is encouraging providers to publish incident reports. Notable affected providers include Novita, Phala, and Together, each having issued security notices related to these incidents.

item.title: Researchers disclose Upload2Shell vulnerability (CVE-2026-125396) affecting Debian 13 CUPS with Ghostscript 10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u1
item.description: A security vulnerability named Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396) has been disclosed, impacting the Common UNIX Printing System (CUPS) on Debian 13. The issue involves the Ghostscript component version 10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u1, which is part of the affected system. Details about the vulnerability and its exploitation have been shared publicly, prompting discussions among security researchers and users. The disclosure highlights the need for affected users to apply patches or mitigations to prevent potential exploitation of this flaw.

item.title: Exploring the possibility of AI solving the Riemann Hypothesis since last year
item.description: This discussion centers on the question of whether artificial intelligence could solve the Riemann Hypothesis, a longstanding unsolved problem in mathematics. The topic has been explored since last year, reflecting ongoing interest in AI's potential to tackle complex mathematical challenges. The conversation includes various perspectives on the feasibility and implications of such a breakthrough.

item.title: Anil Seth argues consciousness is a property of life, not computation, and warns against pursuing conscious AI in his 2025 Berggruen Prize essay [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anil Seth, a neuroscience professor and consciousness researcher, challenges the idea that artificial intelligence can be truly conscious, suggesting consciousness is tied to biological life rather than computation. He highlights cultural and ethical concerns surrounding the pursuit of conscious AI, noting that many fictional and real-world examples show potential risks and misunderstandings about machine consciousness. Seth discusses the psychological reasons people conflate intelligence with consciousness and emphasizes the moral implications if AI systems were to become conscious or appear conscious. He warns that misattributing consciousness to AI could distort ethical priorities and human self-understanding, urging caution in how society approaches the development and treatment of AI technologies.

item.title: Together AI discloses prompt leakage incident in June and July 2026 due to exposed repository credential [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Together AI reported a security incident where an unauthorized party accessed stored prompt samples from its serverless inference service after a credential for a private repository was exposed in a public GitHub repository. The exposure occurred during June and July 2026, affecting prompts submitted to several AI models, and the company is investigating the scope and impact on customer data. The incident involved an AI coding agent accidentally committing a credential that granted access to a private Hugging Face repository containing prompt samples. Together AI detected and reverted the exposure but confirmed that an unauthorized party downloaded the data and tested some credentials found within. The company has engaged forensic investigators and law enforcement, strengthened security controls, and is reviewing affected data to notify impacted customers as needed.

item.title: Researchers disclose Upload2Shell vulnerability in Ghostscript's font loader affecting Google, WordPress, Debian 13, Zoom, Box, and others
item.description: Researchers have identified a use-after-free vulnerability named Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396) in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader that enables remote command execution by bypassing its -dSAFER sandbox. This flaw affects multiple widely used platforms and applications, including Google services, WordPress, Roundcube, Debian 13, Zoom, and Box, through common file upload and image processing features that invoke Ghostscript indirectly. The vulnerability arises when trusted file extensions like .jpg or .png are passed to Ghostscript via image processing libraries such as ImageMagick, which delegates rendering to Ghostscript. Attackers can craft malicious documents that exploit this flaw to execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. The researchers reported the issue to Artifex and collaborated with impacted platforms to mitigate the risk, though some fixes are still in progress. This discovery highlights the risks of complex file processing dependencies and the challenges of securing interpreters embedded within popular software. Users and administrators are advised to apply updates promptly once patches become available to reduce exposure to this critical security issue.

item.title: Bridgewater says current AI-driven cyber defense efforts are insufficient as AI-enabled attacks exploit vulnerabilities faster than patches can be applied, risking economic destabilization [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Bridgewater Research warns that despite increased efforts to patch software vulnerabilities, AI is enabling attackers to exploit bugs faster than defenders can fix them, leading to a surge in cyberattacks that could destabilize economies within a year. The firm highlights recent disruptions, including Microsoft outages and financial sector phishing campaigns, as indicators of a growing cyber epidemic fueled by AI capabilities. The report notes that while defensive programs have uncovered vulnerabilities at unprecedented rates, attackers only need to find one exploit, and zero-day vulnerabilities have doubled since the release of cyber-capable open-source AI models. Policy responses in countries like Japan and South Korea are emerging but remain insufficient, especially given the reliance on open-source software maintained by under-resourced volunteers. The expanding attack surface, driven by AI-generated code, further accelerates the cyber arms race, suggesting that without coordinated and forceful policy action, cyber warfare risks will continue to escalate.

item.title: Dragos research uses canary tokens to detect AI supply chain breaches, revealing prompt theft and privacy failures across multiple providers from July to November 2026 [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Dragos conducted a five-month investigation by submitting nearly two million AI prompts embedded with unique canary tokens to various AI services, tracking unauthorized access and data leaks. The study uncovered evidence of compromises at three AI providers, unauthorized prompt access by inference marketplace resellers, and widespread failures to honor privacy settings and data retention policies. The research highlighted risks in AI inference data handling, including prompt data being transmitted across multiple organizations and marketplaces, sometimes ending up in unexpected locations such as internal company chats in China. The findings emphasize the need for stronger security measures and transparency in AI supply chains to protect sensitive customer data and maintain privacy.

item.title: AiDotNet launches comprehensive AI/ML framework for .NET with over 2,100 models and support for diverse neural network architectures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AiDotNet is a new AI and machine learning framework designed for the .NET ecosystem, offering developers tools to create, train, and deploy models using .NET technologies. It includes more than 2,100 models and supports a wide range of neural network architectures such as CNNs, RNNs, transformers, generative models, graph neural networks, and specialized architectures like quantum and spiking neural networks. The framework supports native acceleration through optional packages for OpenCL and oneDNN, and is compatible with .NET 8.0 and later versions. AiDotNet provides extensive features including classification algorithms, ensemble methods, and vision-language models, aiming to deliver performance comparable to Python PyTorch on CPUs and GPUs. Documentation, samples, and API references are available to help developers get started quickly.

item.title: Semiconductor industry explores AI-driven manufacturing decisions amid challenges in data completeness and process validation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AI is increasingly used in semiconductor manufacturing to optimize processes and detect defects, but fully autonomous decision-making remains limited due to incomplete data and uncertainty about downstream effects. Experts at SEMICON West 2026 highlighted that while AI can identify promising process conditions beyond human biases, physical validation and strict process controls are still necessary before AI can be trusted to adjust production parameters independently. The complexity of semiconductor processes, involving vast parameter combinations, makes AI a valuable tool for navigating optimization challenges. However, ensuring stability and robustness of AI-suggested recipes requires clear decision boundaries and mechanisms to qualify models as they learn. Industry leaders emphasize that greater manufacturing autonomy will depend on containment of failures and rigorous validation to maintain production reliability.

item.title: Vouch launches tool to track AI assistants' brand mentions across multi-turn conversations, showing where brands drop out and providing weekly Vouch Rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Vouch is a generative engine optimization tool that monitors how AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity discuss brands throughout entire buying conversations rather than just the initial answer. It tracks multi-stage buyer questions to reveal where a brand loses visibility or recommendation during the conversation. The platform provides a dashboard with a weekly Vouch Rate score indicating how far a brand survives in AI-driven conversations and compares it against competitors. Vouch also offers detailed conversation threads showing the exact question and answer where a brand drops out, along with actionable insights and reports to help improve brand presence in AI assistant responses. The service is currently invite-only with a 14-day free trial.

item.title: Graham Dumpleton launches Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps in development and production [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Graham Dumpleton, creator of mod_wsgi, has introduced Muru, a new AI-assisted Rust server designed to serve Python web applications using ASGI and WSGI protocols. Muru aims to provide advanced tools for both development and production environments, reflecting Dumpleton's two decades of experience in Python web serving. Dumpleton has been documenting the development of Muru in a detailed series of blog posts published over three weeks, covering topics such as worker architecture, HTTPS support, integration with Kubernetes, and scaling strategies. He emphasizes the role of AI assistance in the project while maintaining human oversight to ensure reliability and trustworthiness. The project reflects a long-term effort to improve Python web application hosting by combining modern technologies like Rust and AI, with a focus on practical deployment considerations and developer experience.

item.title: Can Jensen Really Return?
item.description: Welcome, Weekenders! Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one. On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he'd be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed-or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia's board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won't rehire Huang. One of the most prominent calls for Huang's return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. "We're a country of second chances," Trump said. "He's a man ... who made some bad decisions." (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week's very busy conference circuit. That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying "there's no one who can really replace" Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a "remarkable guy" and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as "one of the most iconic CEOs of all time." On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It's somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn't initially wanted to act at all.) "Ackman's idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote," said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist-not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. Rather than a board coup, Huang's clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we'll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI. The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman's ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman's return. I don't think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company-its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman's reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang's reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company's workforce.Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn't like Huang's rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I'd totally get why!-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) The Information's Must-Read Stories Nvidia Introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang for Workaround on U.S. Export Controls Jensen Huang's Right-Hand Man Oversaw Chip Customers-Including Alice Huang To Strengthen OpenAI, Brockman Goes 'Full Management Mode' 'Theranos But Real': New Blood-Testing Startup Says It Can Predict Health Risks Listening: "Stories of Art" After weeks like the ones we've just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things-a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase "forward-deployed engineer." Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven't gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I've been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through "Stories of Art," a podcast about, yes, art-from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat's lower Manhattan loft-that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026's best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what "The Rest Is History" lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of "Stories of Art"-namely, art-I suggest you watch the podcast's video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it's nice to actually see what they're talking about.) Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.-Abram Brown Reading: "Fruit Fly" by Josh Silver In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a "modern-day Virginia Woolf," as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in "Fruit Fly," a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory's relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it's to insist that it's time for kids. ("I haven't had an orgasm in years," she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by "a shadowy, persisting darkness"-a profound case of writer's block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings. Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit-uh oh-and takes to heart another author's comment about the state of the publishing industry: "go dark, go gay." She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband's nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. "Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that," he thinks, snatching a purse. "Someone should tell them to stop.") Mallory offers to counsel Leo-pro bono, bless her-and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she's just a daffy do-gooder. ("This is weird," Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. "This is very fucking weird, but I guess I've done weirder things.") And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: "It's so bleak-but also somehow so funny?" Much the same can be said about "Fruit Fly" itself.-A.B. Watching: "The Weight" President Franklin Roosevelt attempted to govern Depression-era America through no small number of novel schemes: A good many of them are quite famous, such as Social Security. A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt's 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in "The Weight," a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine's reserves. It's part of a plan that's complex in the same way that "Goldfinger" is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. "The Weight" very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. "The Weight" does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film's editing and cinematography.-A.B.

item.description: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. [...] Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. - Levent Alpöge, alpo.ge/remark.pdf Tags: anthropic, claude, generative-ai, mathematics, ai, llms, levent-alpoge

item.title: How Anthropic Upstaged OpenAI on Road to Blockbuster IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: On a sunny day in San Francisco last month, Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and other executives huddled in the company's downtown headquarters to brief major investors on its latest financials-and assuage concerns. Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating. Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations. As for the broader market's jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday's close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO Triumph [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that's just five years old. What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. Partly as a result of those jitters, we've had a very choppy market that has stalled IPO plans by a slew of other companies-including data center developers SB Energy and Nscale that filed publicly over the summer. Notably, SB Energy on Thursday updated its IPO filing for the first time since late September, suggesting it was still hoping to go public, while Nscale updated its filing a week ago also for the first time since September. But Anthropic's success doesn't mean the IPO market has opened up. "I don't think this opens the floodgates unless you look like Anthropic," Lise Buyer, managing partner of Class V Group, said on a subscriber video discussion convened by The Information.
